rationale: The modest crude build reflects a refinery run cut rather than weak crude supply, while gasoline and distillate draws and firm distillate demand tighten products, so the effect on WTI is two-way and Brent is largely unaffected.
A fifth consecutive OPEC demand cut confirms demand destruction, but it is a three-week-old, already-priced revision with no bearing on this week's balance.
A US diesel export ban would likely cut Gulf Coast runs and US crude demand, which weighs on WTI, while tightening ex-US diesel markets and supporting Brent-linked cracks.
Conflicting reports on a 90-day ban pushed ULSD and refiner equities lower, raising risk to US refinery crude demand, but the White House denial leaves the outcome uncertain.
Intercepted Houthi strikes and reports of US-Iran deal talks produced two-way headline risk, with the deal talk dominating the Brent Nov decline on 25 Sep.
The US rejection of Iran's Hormuz reopening proposal pushed back the diplomatic path to restoring Gulf flows, and Brent rose in Asian trading in response.
Middle East exports recovering toward but still well below pre-war levels ease the crude bottleneck for Brent, while renewed diesel-ban talk adds downside risk to US refinery crude demand.
A large SPR exchange offer would add sour barrels on the Gulf Coast in Nov-Dec, but weak uptake of the June offer makes the actual volume uncertain.
The expiring Brent Nov contract sits at a steep premium to Dec, showing prompt tightness, while a wide Brent-WTI Dec spread and a run-driven crude build leave WTI relatively weaker.
OPEC's 2026 demand downgrade signals visible demand destruction but is backward-looking for this week's balance.
OPEC's higher 2027 growth forecast treats 2026 losses as deferred demand, which mainly supports deferred curve pricing rather than the prompt balance.
A negligible revision to the call on OPEC+ crude is irrelevant while logistics, not quotas, constrain Gulf exports.
A higher 2027 call implies a large OPEC+ output rebuild if transit normalises, which bears on the back of the curve rather than this week.
The August OPEC output rise comes from an unverified third-party summary with offsetting Iraq gains and Iran losses, so it carries little weight.
The IEA's deep demand contraction, far below OPEC's estimate, highlights demand destruction and a wide forecast divergence.
Large global stock draws through August underpin prompt tightness and backwardation, especially in Brent.
The OPEC+ pause in target increases is largely moot while Gulf exports are logistics-limited.
China's crude imports rose for the month but remain well below year-ago levels, giving mild support to seaborne Brent-linked demand.
Higher Chinese refinery runs lift crude demand, though they are currently being supplied partly from onshore stocks.
China's ongoing stock draws show its buffer is cushioning seaborne demand now but may later require restocking imports.
Rising Chinese product exports could ease global diesel tightness at the margin, but estimates vary by source and definition.
China's manufacturing PMI back above 50 is a mildly supportive macro signal for demand sentiment.
